title: Symmetry of the critical current function in superconducting nanodevices
authors: Ziqi Zhao, Cliff Sun, Ci-You Huang, Jiankun Zhang, Xiangyu Song, Alexey Bezryadin
abstract: We study a variety of nano-scale superconducting devices containing more than one weak link. Even in devices with multiple weak links the IB symmetry is usually obeyed, which means that if we reverse both the bias current direction and the magnetic field direction at the same time, the superconducting response, namely the critical current, remains unchanged. We also provide a detailed analysis of the situations in which such symmetry is violated.
summary: This work investigates the symmetry of critical current in nanoscale superconductors using both experiments and advanced theoretical modeling. It establishes that while many multi-link systems obey $I$-$B$ symmetry, hybrid junctions can exhibit clear violations due to polarity-dependent selection among competing vortex states. This has implications for designing reliable superconducting electronic components.
main_problem: The study investigates the symmetry properties of the critical current function ($I_c$) in superconducting nanodevices, specifically focusing on the $I$-$B$ inversion symmetry: $I_{c,+}(B) = -I_{c,-}(-B)$. The goal is to understand when this fundamental symmetry is preserved or broken.
main_result: The $I$-$B$ symmetry is generally obeyed in multi-nanowire SQUID models, but clear violations are observed in hybrid junctions (SIS–ML), suggesting that polarity-dependent selection of metastable vorticity states causes the asymmetry.
method: The research combines low-temperature transport measurements on various nanodevices with theoretical modeling using effective potential energy landscapes derived from Meissner phase equations and Josephson junction physics.
model_or_system: The systems include superconducting weak-link devices (nanowires, SQUIDs) modeled by combining different Current-Phase Relations (CPR), such as sinusoidal (SIS junctions) and linear (metallic links). The analysis focuses on the energy landscape governing vortex configurations.
key_observables: Critical current $I_c(B)$ vs. Magnetic Field $B$, positive ($	ext{Ic}_+$) and negative ($	ext{Ic}_-$) switching currents, and the degree of symmetry matching between $	ext{Ic}_+(B)$ and $-	ext{Ic}_-(-	ext{B})$.
important_parameters: Base temperature ($T_{base} \sim 350$ mK), magnetic field $B$, and junction parameters (e.g., stiffness constants $K_k$).
main_assumptions: For theoretical modeling, approximations include neglecting vector potential contributions along the length of each nanowire (short wire approximation) and assuming specific CPR forms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate SEM images of tested devices; key figures compare measured $	ext{Ic}_+(B)$ vs. $-	ext{Ic}_-(-	ext{B})$ to demonstrate symmetry preservation or type 1/type 2 breaking in hybrid junctions, alongside simulated energy landscapes showing state transitions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from experimental observation of $I$-$B$ symmetry in simple devices (A-C) to identifying clear violations in complex hybrids (D). It then develops theoretical models using multi-nanowire SQUID frameworks and hybrid junction arrays to explain the underlying physics governing state selection and symmetry breaking.
why_interesting: The study bridges fundamental superconducting symmetries with device physics, offering insights into how microscopic details (like junction type or polarity) can break macroscopic symmetries in quantum transport phenomena. This relates to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in mesoscopic circuits.
